EXCLUSIVE INTERVIEW WITH YOLANDE KORKIE

By: Nicky Troll | Delivery

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Yemen Hostage Yolande Korkie's first sit down television interview.

Summary:
14 months after the tragic killing of Pierre Korkie, his wife Yolande is finally ready to share their story in her first on-camera tv interview since her own release in January 2014.

This is a story of supreme love, absolute forgiveness and unwavering faith - exclusively on Carte Blanche.

Further information:
TWO WAYS TO DO IT:
1. It is a bit of scoop getting the first TV one-on-one interview - we can build it up and tell her story of being capture and then separated from her husband - the drama that unfolded in trying to negotiate for his freedom and the tragedy of his death. her story is beautiful in the way her faith kept her going, and even after losing her husband, the father of her children in such a senseless way, she still chooses to forgive.

2.Her interview is not the story (it would be a bit of a waste of an exclusive) and include interviews with Dr. Imitaz Sooliman from Gift of the Givers and an expert hostage negotiator looking at the challenges and dangers that are faced when civilians are left to negotiate hostage releases on their own without any support from governments.


TAKEN HOSTAGE
In May 2013, Pierre Korkie and his wife Yolande were taken hostage by al-Qaeda militants in Ta'iz, Yemen. The couple were abducted when militants mistook them for Americans.

Civilian group – Gift of the Givers worked to accomplish what the South African government had been unable to do: negotiate the release of a South African couple held by Al Qaeda in the lawless desert of southern Yemen. In January, the civilian negotiators succeeded in securing the release of the woman, Yolande Korkie. She was released in January 2014, after 228 days in captivity – Yolande was freed with no ransom requirement.

The couple’s final moments together were rushed, but still remains vivid for Yolande. “We held each other,” wife Yolande said recalling the couple's final moments together. “He could not hear, he said I love you and tell the children I love them.”

The Al-Qaeda group refused to let her husband go, demanding $3 million (about R32.5 million) for him and saying that releasing him without payment would set a bad precedent. According to Sooliman: “They said they would not be able to waive the ransom for Pierre, because ‘if we do it for you, then we will have to do it for everyone.’ ”

In the videos, posted by the nongovernmental organization Gift of the Givers, Yolande Korkie pleaded for the release of her husband. He was an "innocent man, a respected teacher," she said in one.

Yolande Korkie had not heard from her husband since her release and their two children hadn't listened to his voice in the past 18 months.

Early in December there was news that Pierre would be home for Christmas 2015 – but after 558 days of being hostage, Pierre would never make it back to South Africa alive.

Yolande was expecting to reunite with her husband by Christmas. His kidnappers had agreed to return him but that arrangement, brokered by Gift of the Givers, was thwarted by the drone strike. “I visualised something different, him holding me in his arms, hearing his soft voice,” she said of his return.

Asked if she regretted going to Yemen since her husband was killed there, Yolande said she did not. “We have lost but we cannot regret,” she said. “It is God’s will,” she added quietly. Yolande said her husband would never return physically. “But in our hearts he will never die.”

As a family – they choose to forgive. “We choose to love. We choose to rejoice in the memories of Pierre and keep him alive in our hearts. We honour Pierre’s legacy and give Glory to God for his life and death.”

BACKGROUND:
Pierre and Yolande Korkie had been married for 20 years in 2014. The Korkies settled in Yemen in December 2009. Pierre had retired, but continued teaching in Yemen - he was a committed educator, who wanted to help students. Yolande worked in the community doing relief work at a local hospital.

They couple had lived there peacefully for four years with their two teenaged children, until they were captured in 2013.The Department of International Relations and Cooperation (DIRCO) evacuated the children soon after their parents' were captured.

KIDNAPPING IN THE MIDDLE EAST
Kidnapping for ransom has turned into a lucrative business for Al Qaeda and its more extreme offshoot, the Islamic State, an increasing number of Westerners have been abducted. Frustrated by what they see as passive responses from their governments, the families and colleagues of hostages have been thrust into the role of amateur negotiators, initiating contact with the terrorists themselves.

In addition to not paying ransoms, unlike some countries in Europe whose officials have secretly funneled tens of millions of dollars to free their citizens, South Africa and the United States, do not engage in other ways with the terrorist groups holding their citizens.

Mr. Sooliman said Gifts of the Givers felt a moral obligation to help the Korkies — fellow South Africans in harm’s way in a country where the charity had deep ties. Although he said that the South African government had helped with diplomatic hurdles — such as issuing Mr. Korkie a new passport — its policy of non-engagement meant that the charity was on its own in contacting the terrorist group.

RESCUE OPERATION
Using its tribal connections in southern Yemen, Gift of the Givers contacted the kidnappers last year.

After months of silence, Gift of the Givers had a breakthrough in August, when tribal leaders sent a delegation, acting on behalf of the charity, into the remote badlands. The assembled Qaeda fighters took a vote on reducing the ransom, and half the jihadists voted “yes” while half voted “no,” Mr. Sooliman said. In October, the abductors said that they would accept $700,000. The family, which had already said it could not afford $3 million, still did not have enough money.

In November, the tribal leaders went back to meet with Qaeda members. The car was hit by a drone strike, killing the mediators, according to Mr. Sooliman. “We thought it was over,” he said. But that tragedy appears to have spurred Al Qaeda to agree to a lower sum, which it promised to use in part to reimburse families of the dead tribal negotiators. On Nov. 26, Mr. Korkie’s abductors sent word they would accept $200,000, to be split with the tribe members. The money was raised by family, friends and donors.

On the morning of Saturday, 6th December 2014 morning, a convoy of cars was set to leave the southern Yemeni city of Aden to pick up the 54-year-old hostage from the remote outpost where he was being held.

Gift of the Givers had not informed Yemeni officials or the United States of the planned release because their Qaeda contacts had warned them to keep the plans confidential, Mr. Sooliman said.

At 6 a.m. in Johannesburg, Imtiaz Sooliman, the director of the aid group that had led the long effort, sent a text message to Mrs. Korkie: “The waiting is almost over.”
At 8:03 a.m. his phone rang with incomprehensible news: Mr. Korkie was dead.

Hours before his expected release, the South African hostage was killed by his Qaeda guards when a military operation by the United States to save his cellmate — Luke Somers, an American photojournalist — went wrong. Mr. Somers and eight civilians were also killed in the raid.

While Yolande was asleep in SA, President Obama gave the go-ahead for a unit of Navy SEAL Team 6 commandos to try to rescue Mr. Somers after concluding that his life was in imminent danger, because a deadline that his captors had set to meet their demands was about to expire.

It remains unclear what went wrong. Soon after the commandos reached the compound where the hostages were being held, gunfire erupted. Both Mr. Korkie and Mr. Somers were shot by their guards before the commandos could get to them.

United States officials say they did not know that Mr. Korkie was about to be freed, revealing the dangerous disconnect that can occur when civilians are left to negotiate hostage releases on their own. The government of South Africa — like the United States — hews to a strict policy of not paying ransoms to terrorist groups holding their citizens, maintaining that payments encourage kidnappers and perpetuate the problem.

Press Release:


Exclusive: Yolande Korkie
Just over a year ago, Al Qaeda hostage Pierre Korkie was tragically killed during a botched US drone strike in Yemen. South Africans Pierre and his wife Yolande were kidnapped by militants while working in Taiz. In her first television interview since her own release in January 2014, Yolande Korkie speaks exclusively to Carte Blanche about true love, absolute forgiveness and surviving captivity.


Script:


FINAL SCRIPT
UPSOUND: WAR IN YEMEN

VO: The Middle East has been plagued by war for decades, but despite the unrest and violence…Bloemfontein educators Pierre & Yolande Korkie fell in love with Yemen after short visit in 2007.

YOLANDE: We love South Africa and we loved the farm, our hearts had stayed behind in Yemen, with the people..

VO: In 2009 they sold the family farm and moved to the Middle East with their children. After four years of embracing a new life in Yemen, their lives would change forever: Pierre and Yolande were taken hostage by Al Quaeda.

LINK: Two years since her release and a year since her husband was killed in captivity, it’s been a journey of healing and acceptance for Yolande, a story she is finally ready to share in her first television interview.

DEVI: What is like not knowing if there is going to be an end….
YOLANDE: You don’t know when that end is going to be, if there is going to be a finish line, with drones and rockets going off around you – you go back and forth between – am I gonna die know or am I not going to die now. And you get to a point when you stop wondering will tomorrow come – now is important.
DEVI: Did you ever think this could happen to you?
YOLANDE: No, we knew the Americans were more the targets, the Brits and the Europeans. They would be escourted out of the checkpoints, but South Africans, we had a little South African flag in the front of the car, we would just wave the flag and wave goodbye.

VO: They had created a new type of family life in Yemen - Pierre was teaching English, while Yolande ran a riding school and home schooled their children.

DEVI: In your book, you talk about gunfire being pretty normal?
YOLANDE: That became our new normal – that is the amazing thing, one adapts, without noticing //but it’s either a wedding, cause then they blast off their Aks or its either the police shooting at somebody or there is a war going on, a tribal infight going on. Warplanes would come across and we would think, oh, one, two, three, four, five of them oh wow!

VO: In May 2013, Pierre’s dad passed on and the Korkies were heading home for the funeral. But things took an unexpected turn when Yolande and Pierre went to collect their travel documents.

YOLANDE: We were driving down the road, there was a car on the side of us and a car in front of us, so we had to stop, shooting going on across the road, and we looked to where the shooting was going on and we never saw the guys in the middle of the road in amongst the bushes, waiting for us. // the next moment the car was just yanked open . I remember looking back at Pierre, he was just, he had a gun pointed at his head and he watched my kidnapping taking place

VO: Their children were not with them, and were later evacuated by the Department of International Relations, but Pierre and Yolande’s nightmare was just beginning.

YOLANDE: Al Quaeda doesn’t have a place, they don’t have a place to stay. They hide themselves inside a tribe, that is their mask, // as got we got handed over and handed over, we could sense that we were just going deeper and deeper into a lion’s den. It got more dangerous, because they became more nervous, you could see you were getting to the Al Quaeda den. INT 1 M27

LINK: Help came from an unlikely corner, not from government, not from armed forced, but from a South African Humanitarian organisation.

VO: Since 2012, Gift of The Givers have actively been doing aid work in Yemen. Nine months in, local project manager, Anas Al-Hamati got word to the organisation’s founder Dr Imtiaz Sooliman of the Korkies capture.

IMTIAZ: He asked me should we do something, I said look, we’ve got nothing to loose – we are humanitarians,
DEVI: You are a muslim and she is a Christian, but religion played no part here?
IMTIAZ: Islam is very clear – you help human being, irrespective of race, religion, colour, class or creed and you help them unconditionally // The sad part was that people in the name of islam captured her, that spoilt our name, that is not our teaching, that Is not our way.

VO: While Imitiaz and Anas started putting plans in place to find the Korkies, Yolande says every day was about survival for them, they wrote journals and prayed that they would be rescued.

YOLANDE: We were stripped of everything we had on us, by Al Queada – but there was one thing they couldn’t strip, and that was the love we had for each other, the love we had for God and the love He had for us.

VO: Yolande says they grew weak as hostages with very little food and medical treatement. Pierre developed an ear infection, losing his hearing completely.

YOLANDE: We became really just one person. // I would be his ears and he would be me eyes – and what he was thinking I would say and what he was crying about I would feel. //Initially we wouldn’t even sleep, we just wanted that moment to last, the togetherness and being with one another.

VO: In the meantime, the Gift of the Givers had doubled their humanitarian work in Yemen, making it clear with every delivery, that the aid was from South Africa, hoping, that the kidnappers would contact them. Eventually the call came through, the kidnappers wanted to meet.

IMTIAZ: That day when he walked into that building – that’s when he realised this, is AL Quaeda. They told him – you know who we are, we are Al Quaeda, and you know what we are capable of.It’s not about religion, it’s not about politics, it’s about the commodity – it’s a business transaction – so they needed to get their money back at any cost. INT 1 M17
DEVI: They talking big money in the beginning.
IMTIAZ: We know they talk big money We got no money to offer them only have projects….

VO: Using their aid work as leverage, the Gift of the Givers managed to secure Yolande’s release for no ransom whatsoever. But Pierre was to remain a hostage. Yolande recalls those last moments.

YOLANDE: I was in his arms, I was really listening to his heart beating, I felt safe and I felt everything would be ok,

VO: It all happened very quickly…

YOLANDE: It was confusing,stressfull, seconds, we were trying to embrace each other but they kept pulling us apart, and then Pierre pushed away and said just wait, there were no words, were just connecting, and then separated us with the gun…

LINK: After 228 days spent in captivity Yolande was finally freed, but she was not free, she left her heart behind.

YOLANDE: It’s unreal to see Yemen slipping away – Pierre is somewhere down there in the sand, I was also looking forward to see the children, I wanted to get out and push the airplane, but at the same time I wanted to turn around – I was torn apart – I was going but staying, going but staying.

VO: But Yolande’s ordeal was far from over says Imtiaz.

IMTIAZ: But when they released her they put a huge burden on her head. They said you have 8 days to arrange $3million days otherwise Pierre’s head will be sent to you in a box.

VO: She immediately switched gears and started working on securing Pierre’s release, even uploading a plea for his life.

UPSOUND: Pleases for his release….

VO: The deadline passed and Pierre’s life was spared. Close to 11 months later his release was secured, with the help of tribal leaders that Anas had canvassed in Yemen – no ransom was to be paid, but a $110 000 facilitation fee was due.

IMTIAZ: This is different from ransom – ransom you pay upfront, the facilitation money you pay only after we deliver the package.

VO: With the war intesifying between Al Quaeda and Yemeni civilians, Imtiaz was nervous that there might be an American attack any day, he urged Anas to move up the exchange.

IMTIAZ: he said we can’t go in there’s fighting everything – I said phone the tribal leaders now and make sure the money is ready – you have to go in otherwsie you wasted the whole year. He said you’re crazy! I said it has to be done. 06.00 morning Anas said we are ready.
YOLANDE: I think I hardly slept that night, // just before six, Imtiaz and I had a whatsapp conversation and his last words to me was – the waits almost over Yolande.

VO: Her phone rang at 07.00, it was the specialist kidnap truama counsellor from the police

YOLANDE: CRIES …Col Strydom called, the wait was over – he was free but not free as we imagined,

VO: After 558 days in captivity - Pierre was killed in a botched US rescue operation of an american hostage. Although the details are sketchy, Yolande has found acceptance…

YOLANDE: It doesn’t matter any more, I can’t ever turn back the clock, it’s finished….

VO: Pierre’s body was returned to South Africa for his burial, along with the journals he had kept after Yolande’s release.

YOLANDE: Reading those journals put me back there, and I had to go through those emotions again, hope, no hope…
DEVI: What was he thinking?
YOLANDE: It was really hard for him // it was hard to stay behind
DEVI: Did it break your heart?
YOLANDE: It broke my heart, it really did, it made me almost stop writing, I was not going to continue.

DEVI: Together you could take on the world, but now alone.
YOLANDE: Alone it was difficult, I kept reminding myself what Pierre would have said now, how he would encourage me, this separation can’t separate the love that we had.


 
PROMOS

PROMO 1 – 10 seconds
VO: We bring you an exclusive interview with Yemen Hostage survivor Yolande Korkie.

YOLANDE: we were just going deeper and deeper into a lion’s den


PROMO 2 – 15 seconds
VO: 14 months after the tragic killing of Pierre Korkie, his wife Yolande shares their story in her first TV interview since her own release.

YOLANDE: The wait was over – he was free but not free as we imagined.


PROMO 3 – 15 seconds
VO: Hostage survivor Yolande Korkie shares her story of love, faith and forgiveness.

YOLANDE: We were stripped of everything by Al Quade, but there was one thing they couldn’t strip, and that was the love we had for each other, the love we had for God and the love He had for us.

Carte Blanche HD Nikola Vrahimis 29 February 2016 Press Release: Exclusive: Yolande Korkie Just over a year ago, Al Qaeda hostage Pierre Korkie was tragically killed during a botched US drone strike in Yemen. South Africans Pierre and his wife Yolande were kidnapped by militants while working in Taiz. In her first television interview since her own release in January 2014, Yolande Korkie speaks exclusively to Carte Blanche about true love, absolute forgiveness and surviving captivity. Script: FINAL SCRIPT UPSOUND: WAR IN YEMEN VO: The Middle East has been plagued by war for decades, but despite the unrest and violence…Bloemfontein educators Pierre & Yolande Korkie fell in love with Yemen after short visit in 2007. YOLANDE: We love South Africa and we loved the farm, our hearts had stayed behind in Yemen, with the people.. VO: In 2009 they sold the family farm and moved to the Middle East with their children. After four years of embracing a new life in Yemen, their lives would change forever: Pierre and Yolande were taken hostage by Al Quaeda. LINK: Two years since her release and a year since her husband was killed in captivity, it’s been a journey of healing and acceptance for Yolande, a story she is finally ready to share in her first television interview. DEVI: What is like not knowing if there is going to be an end…. YOLANDE: You don’t know when that end is going to be, if there is going to be a finish line, with drones and rockets going off around you – you go back and forth between – am I gonna die know or am I not going to die now. And you get to a point when you stop wondering will tomorrow come – now is important. DEVI: Did you ever think this could happen to you? YOLANDE: No, we knew the Americans were more the targets, the Brits and the Europeans. They would be escourted out of the checkpoints, but South Africans, we had a little South African flag in the front of the car, we would just wave the flag and wave goodbye. VO: They had created a new type of family life in Yemen - Pierre was teaching English, while Yolande ran a riding school and home schooled their children. DEVI: In your book, you talk about gunfire being pretty normal? YOLANDE: That became our new normal – that is the amazing thing, one adapts, without noticing //but it’s either a wedding, cause then they blast off their Aks or its either the police shooting at somebody or there is a war going on, a tribal infight going on. Warplanes would come across and we would think, oh, one, two, three, four, five of them oh wow! VO: In May 2013, Pierre’s dad passed on and the Korkies were heading home for the funeral. But things took an unexpected turn when Yolande and Pierre went to collect their travel documents. YOLANDE: We were driving down the road, there was a car on the side of us and a car in front of us, so we had to stop, shooting going on across the road, and we looked to where the shooting was going on and we never saw the guys in the middle of the road in amongst the bushes, waiting for us. // the next moment the car was just yanked open . I remember looking back at Pierre, he was just, he had a gun pointed at his head and he watched my kidnapping taking place VO: Their children were not with them, and were later evacuated by the Department of International Relations, but Pierre and Yolande’s nightmare was just beginning. YOLANDE: Al Quaeda doesn’t have a place, they don’t have a place to stay. They hide themselves inside a tribe, that is their mask, // as got we got handed over and handed over, we could sense that we were just going deeper and deeper into a lion’s den. It got more dangerous, because they became more nervous, you could see you were getting to the Al Quaeda den. INT 1 M27 LINK: Help came from an unlikely corner, not from government, not from armed forced, but from a South African Humanitarian organisation. VO: Since 2012, Gift of The Givers have actively been doing aid work in Yemen. Nine months in, local project manager, Anas Al-Hamati got word to the organisation’s founder Dr Imtiaz Sooliman of the Korkies capture. IMTIAZ: He asked me should we do something, I said look, we’ve got nothing to loose – we are humanitarians, DEVI: You are a muslim and she is a Christian, but religion played no part here? IMTIAZ: Islam is very clear – you help human being, irrespective of race, religion, colour, class or creed and you help them unconditionally // The sad part was that people in the name of islam captured her, that spoilt our name, that is not our teaching, that Is not our way. VO: While Imitiaz and Anas started putting plans in place to find the Korkies, Yolande says every day was about survival for them, they wrote journals and prayed that they would be rescued. YOLANDE: We were stripped of everything we had on us, by Al Queada – but there was one thing they couldn’t strip, and that was the love we had for each other, the love we had for God and the love He had for us. VO: Yolande says they grew weak as hostages with very little food and medical treatement. Pierre developed an ear infection, losing his hearing completely. YOLANDE: We became really just one person. // I would be his ears and he would be me eyes – and what he was thinking I would say and what he was crying about I would feel. //Initially we wouldn’t even sleep, we just wanted that moment to last, the togetherness and being with one another. VO: In the meantime, the Gift of the Givers had doubled their humanitarian work in Yemen, making it clear with every delivery, that the aid was from South Africa, hoping, that the kidnappers would contact them. Eventually the call came through, the kidnappers wanted to meet. IMTIAZ: That day when he walked into that building – that’s when he realised this, is AL Quaeda. They told him – you know who we are, we are Al Quaeda, and you know what we are capable of.It’s not about religion, it’s not about politics, it’s about the commodity – it’s a business transaction – so they needed to get their money back at any cost. INT 1 M17 DEVI: They talking big money in the beginning. IMTIAZ: We know they talk big money We got no money to offer them only have projects…. VO: Using their aid work as leverage, the Gift of the Givers managed to secure Yolande’s release for no ransom whatsoever. But Pierre was to remain a hostage. Yolande recalls those last moments. YOLANDE: I was in his arms, I was really listening to his heart beating, I felt safe and I felt everything would be ok, VO: It all happened very quickly… YOLANDE: It was confusing,stressfull, seconds, we were trying to embrace each other but they kept pulling us apart, and then Pierre pushed away and said just wait, there were no words, were just connecting, and then separated us with the gun… LINK: After 228 days spent in captivity Yolande was finally freed, but she was not free, she left her heart behind. YOLANDE: It’s unreal to see Yemen slipping away – Pierre is somewhere down there in the sand, I was also looking forward to see the children, I wanted to get out and push the airplane, but at the same time I wanted to turn around – I was torn apart – I was going but staying, going but staying. VO: But Yolande’s ordeal was far from over says Imtiaz. IMTIAZ: But when they released her they put a huge burden on her head. They said you have 8 days to arrange $3million days otherwise Pierre’s head will be sent to you in a box. VO: She immediately switched gears and started working on securing Pierre’s release, even uploading a plea for his life. UPSOUND: Pleases for his release…. VO: The deadline passed and Pierre’s life was spared. Close to 11 months later his release was secured, with the help of tribal leaders that Anas had canvassed in Yemen – no ransom was to be paid, but a $110 000 facilitation fee was due. IMTIAZ: This is different from ransom – ransom you pay upfront, the facilitation money you pay only after we deliver the package. VO: With the war intesifying between Al Quaeda and Yemeni civilians, Imtiaz was nervous that there might be an American attack any day, he urged Anas to move up the exchange. IMTIAZ: he said we can’t go in there’s fighting everything – I said phone the tribal leaders now and make sure the money is ready – you have to go in otherwsie you wasted the whole year. He said you’re crazy! I said it has to be done. 06.00 morning Anas said we are ready. YOLANDE: I think I hardly slept that night, // just before six, Imtiaz and I had a whatsapp conversation and his last words to me was – the waits almost over Yolande. VO: Her phone rang at 07.00, it was the specialist kidnap truama counsellor from the police YOLANDE: CRIES …Col Strydom called, the wait was over – he was free but not free as we imagined, VO: After 558 days in captivity - Pierre was killed in a botched US rescue operation of an american hostage. Although the details are sketchy, Yolande has found acceptance… YOLANDE: It doesn’t matter any more, I can’t ever turn back the clock, it’s finished…. VO: Pierre’s body was returned to South Africa for his burial, along with the journals he had kept after Yolande’s release. YOLANDE: Reading those journals put me back there, and I had to go through those emotions again, hope, no hope… DEVI: What was he thinking? YOLANDE: It was really hard for him // it was hard to stay behind DEVI: Did it break your heart? YOLANDE: It broke my heart, it really did, it made me almost stop writing, I was not going to continue. DEVI: Together you could take on the world, but now alone. YOLANDE: Alone it was difficult, I kept reminding myself what Pierre would have said now, how he would encourage me, this separation can’t separate the love that we had. PROMOS PROMO 1 – 10 seconds VO: We bring you an exclusive interview with Yemen Hostage survivor Yolande Korkie. YOLANDE: we were just going deeper and deeper into a lion’s den PROMO 2 – 15 seconds VO: 14 months after the tragic killing of Pierre Korkie, his wife Yolande shares their story in her first TV interview since her own release. YOLANDE: The wait was over – he was free but not free as we imagined. PROMO 3 – 15 seconds VO: Hostage survivor Yolande Korkie shares her story of love, faith and forgiveness. YOLANDE: We were stripped of everything by Al Quade, but there was one thing they couldn’t strip, and that was the love we had for each other, the love we had for God and the love He had for us. metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Yemen Hostage Yolande Korkie's first sit down television interview.
metadata.Summary: 14 months after the tragic killing of Pierre Korkie, his wife Yolande is finally ready to share their story in her first on-camera tv interview since her own release in January 2014. This is a story of supreme love, absolute forgiveness and unwavering faith - exclusively on Carte Blanche.
metadata.Further information: TWO WAYS TO DO IT: 1. It is a bit of scoop getting the first TV one-on-one interview - we can build it up and tell her story of being capture and then separated from her husband - the drama that unfolded in trying to negotiate for his freedom and the tragedy of his death. her story is beautiful in the way her faith kept her going, and even after losing her husband, the father of her children in such a senseless way, she still chooses to forgive. 2.Her interview is not the story (it would be a bit of a waste of an exclusive) and include interviews with Dr. Imitaz Sooliman from Gift of the Givers and an expert hostage negotiator looking at the challenges and dangers that are faced when civilians are left to negotiate hostage releases on their own without any support from governments. TAKEN HOSTAGE In May 2013, Pierre Korkie and his wife Yolande were taken hostage by al-Qaeda militants in Ta'iz, Yemen. The couple were abducted when militants mistook them for Americans. Civilian group – Gift of the Givers worked to accomplish what the South African government had been unable to do: negotiate the release of a South African couple held by Al Qaeda in the lawless desert of southern Yemen. In January, the civilian negotiators succeeded in securing the release of the woman, Yolande Korkie. She was released in January 2014, after 228 days in captivity – Yolande was freed with no ransom requirement. The couple’s final moments together were rushed, but still remains vivid for Yolande. “We held each other,” wife Yolande said recalling the couple's final moments together. “He could not hear, he said I love you and tell the children I love them.” The Al-Qaeda group refused to let her husband go, demanding $3 million (about R32.5 million) for him and saying that releasing him without payment would set a bad precedent. According to Sooliman: “They said they would not be able to waive the ransom for Pierre, because ‘if we do it for you, then we will have to do it for everyone.’ ” In the videos, posted by the nongovernmental organization Gift of the Givers, Yolande Korkie pleaded for the release of her husband. He was an "innocent man, a respected teacher," she said in one. Yolande Korkie had not heard from her husband since her release and their two children hadn't listened to his voice in the past 18 months. Early in December there was news that Pierre would be home for Christmas 2015 – but after 558 days of being hostage, Pierre would never make it back to South Africa alive. Yolande was expecting to reunite with her husband by Christmas. His kidnappers had agreed to return him but that arrangement, brokered by Gift of the Givers, was thwarted by the drone strike. “I visualised something different, him holding me in his arms, hearing his soft voice,” she said of his return. Asked if she regretted going to Yemen since her husband was killed there, Yolande said she did not. “We have lost but we cannot regret,” she said. “It is God’s will,” she added quietly. Yolande said her husband would never return physically. “But in our hearts he will never die.” As a family – they choose to forgive. “We choose to love. We choose to rejoice in the memories of Pierre and keep him alive in our hearts. We honour Pierre’s legacy and give Glory to God for his life and death.” BACKGROUND: Pierre and Yolande Korkie had been married for 20 years in 2014. The Korkies settled in Yemen in December 2009. Pierre had retired, but continued teaching in Yemen - he was a committed educator, who wanted to help students. Yolande worked in the community doing relief work at a local hospital. They couple had lived there peacefully for four years with their two teenaged children, until they were captured in 2013.The Department of International Relations and Cooperation (DIRCO) evacuated the children soon after their parents' were captured. KIDNAPPING IN THE MIDDLE EAST Kidnapping for ransom has turned into a lucrative business for Al Qaeda and its more extreme offshoot, the Islamic State, an increasing number of Westerners have been abducted. Frustrated by what they see as passive responses from their governments, the families and colleagues of hostages have been thrust into the role of amateur negotiators, initiating contact with the terrorists themselves. In addition to not paying ransoms, unlike some countries in Europe whose officials have secretly funneled tens of millions of dollars to free their citizens, South Africa and the United States, do not engage in other ways with the terrorist groups holding their citizens. Mr. Sooliman said Gifts of the Givers felt a moral obligation to help the Korkies — fellow South Africans in harm’s way in a country where the charity had deep ties. Although he said that the South African government had helped with diplomatic hurdles — such as issuing Mr. Korkie a new passport — its policy of non-engagement meant that the charity was on its own in contacting the terrorist group. RESCUE OPERATION Using its tribal connections in southern Yemen, Gift of the Givers contacted the kidnappers last year. After months of silence, Gift of the Givers had a breakthrough in August, when tribal leaders sent a delegation, acting on behalf of the charity, into the remote badlands. The assembled Qaeda fighters took a vote on reducing the ransom, and half the jihadists voted “yes” while half voted “no,” Mr. Sooliman said. In October, the abductors said that they would accept $700,000. The family, which had already said it could not afford $3 million, still did not have enough money. In November, the tribal leaders went back to meet with Qaeda members. The car was hit by a drone strike, killing the mediators, according to Mr. Sooliman. “We thought it was over,” he said. But that tragedy appears to have spurred Al Qaeda to agree to a lower sum, which it promised to use in part to reimburse families of the dead tribal negotiators. On Nov. 26, Mr. Korkie’s abductors sent word they would accept $200,000, to be split with the tribe members. The money was raised by family, friends and donors. On the morning of Saturday, 6th December 2014 morning, a convoy of cars was set to leave the southern Yemeni city of Aden to pick up the 54-year-old hostage from the remote outpost where he was being held. Gift of the Givers had not informed Yemeni officials or the United States of the planned release because their Qaeda contacts had warned them to keep the plans confidential, Mr. Sooliman said. At 6 a.m. in Johannesburg, Imtiaz Sooliman, the director of the aid group that had led the long effort, sent a text message to Mrs. Korkie: “The waiting is almost over.” At 8:03 a.m. his phone rang with incomprehensible news: Mr. Korkie was dead. Hours before his expected release, the South African hostage was killed by his Qaeda guards when a military operation by the United States to save his cellmate — Luke Somers, an American photojournalist — went wrong. Mr. Somers and eight civilians were also killed in the raid. While Yolande was asleep in SA, President Obama gave the go-ahead for a unit of Navy SEAL Team 6 commandos to try to rescue Mr. Somers after concluding that his life was in imminent danger, because a deadline that his captors had set to meet their demands was about to expire. It remains unclear what went wrong. Soon after the commandos reached the compound where the hostages were being held, gunfire erupted. Both Mr. Korkie and Mr. Somers were shot by their guards before the commandos could get to them. United States officials say they did not know that Mr. Korkie was about to be freed, revealing the dangerous disconnect that can occur when civilians are left to negotiate hostage releases on their own. The government of South Africa — like the United States — hews to a strict policy of not paying ransoms to terrorist groups holding their citizens, maintaining that payments encourage kidnappers and perpetuate the problem.
